title: Odile and the Glasshouse
premise: For twelve years, Paloma Zhou has mailed unsent confessions as postcards to the Zhou family glasshouse, which burned down in a fire that killed her aunt — a fire Paloma believes she caused by a single delayed warning. When a stranger named Odile appears at the matriarch's funeral calling the family by their true surname, Wei, Paloma discovers the woman in the old photographs is not the servant the family remembers but the daughter the Weis erased. As the estate sale looms, Odile and Paloma excavate the fire's true cause: the matriarch herself locked the doors to punish a betrayal, and the servant — Odile's mother — died covering for the family's silence. Paloma must choose between the loyalty she owes the dead and the truth she owes the living, and the novel ends with her testifying at the sale hearing, the estate preserved as a memorial, and Paloma finally writing one last postcard — addressed, this time, to a living person.
about_author: Edmund Voss is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the estates of families that no longer exist, a job that taught him how much of a life is stored in what gets left out. He writes from a coastal town where the fog arrives earlier every year, and where, he insists, the mail is unreliable in instructive ways.

chapters.title: Postcards to a Burnt Address
chapters.summary: Paloma, in first person, writes her weekly postcard to the glasshouse's ruined address and prepares for her grandmother's funeral. Flashbacks reveal her ritual of 'almost saying it.' The emotional beat is quiet dread: the funeral will gather everyone she has spent twelve years not confessing to.

chapters.title: The Stranger Who Knew the Other Name
chapters.summary: At the funeral, an older woman signs the book as Odile Wei — a surname the family abandoned decades ago. Paloma's uncle confronts her; Odile says only, 'I've come about the photographs.' The beat is disruption: the sealed family story cracks open in public.

chapters.title: What the Album Wouldn't Show
chapters.summary: Paloma raids the family album and finds a woman cropped from every frame, edges of her still visible. A cousin admits the 'housekeeper' was the matriarch's half-sister. The beat is vertigo: the family Paloma served has been lying longer than she has.

chapters.title: Odile, In Her Own Weather
chapters.summary: Shifting to Odile's third-person POV, she arrives in town with her mother's letters and a lawyer's letter of her own: a claim against the estate. She is not seeking money but acknowledgment. The beat is resolve sharpened by grief.

chapters.title: The Terms of the Sale
chapters.summary: Paloma learns the estate sale closes in six weeks; the developer's plans will bulldoze the glasshouse ruins. The uncle offers Paloma a share of the proceeds — contingent on her silence about the fire. The beat is complicity offered as love.

chapters.title: Convergence at the Ruins
chapters.summary: Odile and Paloma meet at the glasshouse remains and trade their inheritances: Odile's mother's letters, Paloma's twelve years of postcards. Each realizes the other has been writing to the same silence. The beat is reluctant recognition.

chapters.title: The Night of the Fire, Reassembled
chapters.summary: Piecing letters against Paloma's memory, they reconstruct the truth: the matriarch locked the glasshouse to punish a betrayal, and Odile's mother died helping others out — including young Paloma, whose delayed warning she never blamed. The beat is devastating reversal: Paloma's guilt was misdirected.

chapters.title: Loyalty Is a Kind of Lie
chapters.summary: Paloma confronts the dying uncle, who confesses he helped his mother lock the doors and has paid Paloma's silence ever since. He begs her to let the dead stay buried. The beat is the novel's moral crux: loyalty versus truth, with money as the hinge.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: At the estate sale hearing, Paloma testifies to the fire's true circumstances and Odile files her claim; the uncle, present in a wheelchair, does not deny it. The sale is stayed pending inquiry. The beat is climax — justice achieved outside the law's original design, through speech.

chapters.title: One Last Postcard, Properly Addressed
chapters.summary: Months later, the glasshouse is designated a memorial; Odile stays to curate it. Paloma writes her final postcard — to Odile, at a real address — and for the first time says the thing outright. The beat is forgiveness given and received, the almost-said finally said.
